case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 20th day of June, 2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1447 of 1998).
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. This Civil Appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 20.06.2006 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 144 of 1998 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and order dated 10.03.1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Tangail, in Miscellaneous No.38 of 1996 allowing the appeal upon reversing those dated 28.07.1996 of the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Mirzapur, in Pre-emption Case No.44 of 1994 allowing pre-emption.

2. Facts giving rise to this civil appeal in short are:

3. That respondent No.1 herein, as Pre-emptor, filed Pre-emption Case No. 44 of 1994 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Mirzapur, Tangail, for pre-empting .48 acre out of 1.51 acre of land in Plot Nos. 5/9/11 of RS Khatian No. 198 and CS Khatian No. 122 situated in Mouza Chhitmamudpur, PS-Mirzapur, Tangail, stating, inter alia, that 14.37 acres of land in C.S Khatian No. 122 originally belonged to two brothers, namely, Osimuddin and Kasimuddin, both sons of late Boksha Mollah, in equal share. While they were in peaceful enjoyment of the same Osimuddin died leaving behind 3(three) sons, namely, Abdul Kuddus Mollah, Abdul Mollah and Ramjan Mollah as his heirs who were possessing the same peacefully in ejmali and got their names finally recorded in the ROR Khatian. Thereafter, Abdul Mollah died leaving behind four sons namely, Sobdar Mollah, Yakub Mollah, Badar MollEih and Nurul Mollah and one daughter, namely Most. Sharifunnessa (respondent Nos. 16-19 and 32 respectively), as his legal heirs. While, in peaceful enjoyment of the same, all the said heirs of Abdul Mollah transferred 1.80 acres of land in Dag No. 392, Khatian No. 123, including the case land in separate Dag Nos. 5/8/9/10/11, Khatian No. 122, to the pre-emptor-respondent No.1 by exchange deed dated 04.01.1988. Accordingly the pre-emptor took over possession thereof and became a co sharer tenant in the case jote along with Kuddus Mollah and others. In the meantime Kuddus Mollah, brother of Abdul Mollah, sold .48 acre of land to Dr. Forman Ali Miah (preemptee-appellant), by registered deed dated 15.06.1994, without giving any statutory notice to the pre-emptor. The Pre-emptee-appellant is thus a stranger purchaser. Hence, the pre-emptor respondent No.1 filed the aforesaid pre-emption case in respect of the said .48 acre of land.

4. The pre-emptee-appellant contested the said case by filing written objection, contending inter-alia, that 14.37 acres of land originally belonged to Boksha Mollah who died leaving behind two sons Osimuddin and Kasimuddin as his heirs whose names were recorded in equal share. Osimuddin died leaving 3 sons, namely, Abdul Mollah, Kuddus Mollah, and Ramjan Mollah as his heirs. While in peaceful enjoyment of the same, Kuddus Mollah and Ramjan Mollah, the two brothers of late Abdul Mollah sold 2.88 acres of land from case Plots No. 5/9 along with other plots to Ghutu Sikdar, father of pre-emptee appellant, by registered deed dated 31.08.1945 and handed over possession of the same to him. Thereafter, while in possession of the same Ghutu Sikdar transferred .80 acre of land from case plots No. 5/9 along with other plots to his son, the appellant by a registered Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 01.11.1988 and handed over possession in his favour. Accordingly the pre-emptee-appellant became a cc sharer-tenant by purchase of the said case land, even otherwise than by purchase'. On the other hand, the said Kuddus Mollah subsequently by another registered deed dated 15.06.1994 sold the case land measuring .48 acre from Plots No. 5/9/11 to the pre-emptee-appellant and handed over possession of the same in his favour. Since then the pre-emptee appellant is possessing the same in ejmali upon erecting dwelling house thereon. On the other hand the pre-emptor respondent after purchasing 1.80 acres of land from Plots No. 5/8/9/10/11 in 1988 is possessing the same upon mutating his name vide Mutation Miscellaneous Case No. 1063(IX-1) of 1990-91 and accordingly, got a separate Khatian/holding in his nale and therefore the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case jote and as such the pre-emption case is not maintainable.

5. The learned Assistant Judge, after hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record, allowed the pre-emption case on contest with direction upon the pre-emptee appellant to handover the case land to the pre-emptor respondent No.1 within 45 days in default to take possession of the same through Court, by judgment and order dated 28.07.1996.

6. The pre-emptee-appellant challenged the said judgment and order in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 1996 before the learned District Judge, Tangail which was ultimately heard and allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge (Now Joint District Judge) and Artharin Adalat, Tangail, by judgment and order dated 18.03.1998. Against which the pre-emptor respondent No.1 moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1447 of 1998 and obtained Rule.

7. A Single Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute and set aside the judgment and order dated 18.03.1998 passed by the court of appeal below and upheld the judgment and order dated 28.7.1996 passed by the trial Court in Pre-emption Case No. 44 of 1994, by the impugned judgment and order dated 20.06.2006. Hence the pre-emptee-appellant preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1703 of 2007 and obtained leave which gave rise to the instant appeal.

<u>8. Mr. Subrata Saha, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant submits that the pre-emptor respondent No.1, Nizamuddin, purchased the land in the jote from the heirs of Abdul Mollah whereas Ghutu Shikder, father of the pre-emptee-appellant, Dr Forman All Miah, purchased 2.88 acres of land in case jote from Kuddus Mollah and Ramjan Mollah, brothers of late Mollah and thereafter transferred .80 acre to the appellant in 1988 thus the appellant became co-sharer in the case jote otherwise by purchase. Therefore, the status of the preemptee and the pre-emptor of the case jote is the same. The learned Advocate further submits that Ghutu S'kdar also sold .24 acre of land to the pre-emptor Nizamuddin at the same time when he transferred .80 acre of land to his son, Dr. Forman Ali Miah. Therefore, in this respect also the status of the pre-emptee and the pre-emptor is the same. The learned Advocate finally submits that the High Court Division commit-ted error in not holding teat failing to pro-duce the process server of the notice upon the co-sharers for the purpose of mutation case, is not the proof of non-service of notice. In this respect Mr. Saha submits that for determination of this question the trial court could have called for the record of the mutation case and without doing so, it cannot be said that notice was not served upon the co-sharers as it is the settled principle of law that any person, who denies a public document like certified copy, the burden of proof lies upon him to prove the same. Accordingly he prayed that the appeal should be allowed.</u>

9. Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor-respondent No.1 submits that the respondent is a co-sharer tenant by Ewaznama (Exchange Deed) dated 04.01.1988 and he is also a co-sharer by purchase from the father of the appellant. As such he submits that the High Court Division did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment which is based on proper appreciation of section 96 as well as section 10 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Hence he submits that this appeal should be dismissed.

10. From the above noted submissions of both the sides and on perusal of the materials on record, including the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, it appears that admittedly the case land is an agricultural land and the preemptor respondent, claiming to be a co-sharer-tenant in the case jote by way of exchange and purchase, filed the pre-emption case. He alleged that the preemptee-appellant is a stranger purchaser in the case jote and as such the pre-emptor has right to pre-empt the case land.

11. It also appears that the pre-emptee-appellant's father, Ghutu Sikdar, purchased 2.88 acres of case land from Kuddus Mollah and Ramjan Mollah the two brothers of late Abdul Mollah, all sons of late Osimuddin Mollah who inherited the same from their father late Boksha Mollah. After purchase Ghutu Sikder transferred .80 acre of land to his son, Dr. Forman Ali Miah, (the pre-emptee appellant), by Heba-bil-Ewaz dated 01.11.1988. On the other hand the said Kuddus Mollah transferred .48 acre of case land to the pre-emptee by kabala dated 16.6.1994 and handed over the possession of the same to him and as such the pre-emptee appellant claimed that thus he also became the co-sharer-tenant of the case jote otherwise than by purchase' since long. The pre-emptee claims that since the case land is uneven land, he, after purchasing the same, developed it by earth filling and by planting trees by spending TK.50,000/=. The pre-emptee claimed that he has land in Plot No. 8 which is adjacent to the case Plot No. 5 on the southern side of which he has homestead whereas the pre-emptor has no land nearer, adjacent or surrounding the case plot. Thus he has no necessity of the case land. It is also claimed that the pre-emptor respondent No. 1 after purchasing 1.80 acre of land got his name mutated by opening a separate holding with the Office of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Mirzapur, Tangail, vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1063(IX-I) 90-91 and accordingly paying rents to the government. Thus the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer nor has any nexus with the case jote. The pre-emptee appellant claims that although by kabala of the same date i.e. 15.6.1994 Kuddus Mollah also transferred .34 acre of land adjacent to case Plot No.9 to one Abdul Kader, but the pre-emptor respondent No.1 did not file any pre-emption case over the said land. Accordingly he claimed that the present pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed.

12. Under such circumstances leave has been granted to consider as to (I)'whether the status of the pre-emptor respondent No.1 and that of the pre-emptee-appellant is same'; (II) whether 'the High Court Division committed wrong in not holding that failing to produce the process server of the service of notice upon the co-sharers, for the purpose of mutation case is not the proof of non-servicing of notice'; and (III) whether 'for determination of the question as to non service of notice upon the co-sharer the trial Court should have called for the record of the mutation case and without doing so whether it can’t be said that the notice was not served upon the co-sharers'.

<u>13. As to the first point 'whether the status of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee is same', it appears that the pre-emptor respondent No.1 got 1.80 acre of land from case plots No. 5/8/9/10/11 by Deed of Exchange dated 04.01.1988 from the heirs of Abdul Mollah. On the other hand, the pre-emptee appellant got .80 acre of land from case Plots No. 5/9 from his father Ghutu Sikder by way of Heba-Bill Ewaz dated 01.11.1988 out of 2.88 acre of land which he purchased from Kuddus Mollah and his brother Ramjan Mollah the other brothers of Abdul Mollah who inherited the same from their father and possessing in ejmali. So it appears that the pre-emptee is one of the existing co sharers in the case jote since 1988 even then the impugned purchase on 15.6.1994. On the other hand the pre-emptor after getting 1.80 acre of land by exchange .got his purchased land separated by opening a different holding/khatian through mutation and paying rents to the government for which he cannot be treated a co-sharer in the case jote and hence he has no right to file pre-emption case as a co-sharer, in the case land under the law. When a person by opening a separate khatian got his holding separated and paying rents accordingly, he cannot be treated as a co-sharer in the same case jote and as such he cannot pre-empt any land of the earlier jote under section 96 read with section 117(1 C) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

14. In determining other two points as to (II) 'whether failing to produce the process server of the service of notice upon the co-sharers for the purpose of mutation case is not the proof of non-service of notice and (III) for determination of the question as to non service of notice upon the co-sharer whether the trial Court should have called for the record of the mutation case and in not doing so whether it can be said that the notice was not served upon the co-sharers', we need to go through the evidences of the PWs and OPWs. In this respect PW.1, Md. Nizamuddin Miah the pre-emptor, deposed that he did not get his name mutated by opening a separate holding. In Cross he stated that it is not true that he filed the application with the office of the Mirzapur Revenue Office for get-ting his name mutated. On the other hand, OPW-1, the pre-emptee deposed that the pre-emptor got his name mutated by opening a separate holding vide Miscellaneous Case No. 1063/1990-91 and in support of his deposition he produced certified copy of the said mutation case and rather the pre-emptee upon getting .80 acre of land from his father in 1988 and after purchase of the said case land in 1994 is a co sharer in the case jote. However, to prove the claim that the pre-emptor got his land separated and opened a separate khatian vide above noted mutation case the pre-emptee filed certified copy of the said mutation khatian in the name of the pre-emptor(Exhibit-'Kha'). But on the face of denial by the pre-emptor, the trial Court held

"এই জমা ভাগের উপর স্বাক্ষ্য প্রদান করা কালে প্রতিপক্ষ আঃ ফরমান আলী প্রতিপক্ষের ১নং সাক্ষীর জেরায় বলেন উক্ত জমাভাগের কেসের উপর কোন শরীক নোটিশ পাইবার প্রমান তাহার কাছে নাই। আর জমাভাগ হইতে হইলে অবশ্যই সকল শরীকের প্রতি নোটিশ জারী হওয়া বাঞ্জনীয়। তাহা ছাড়া দাখিলী আদেশেও কেহ হাজির হইয়াছেন মর্মে উল্লেখ নাই। এই অবস্থায় ইহাকে বিধি সম্মত জমাভাগ বলা য়ায় না।" Hence the trial Court disbelieved the mutation.

<u>15. When the pre-emptee appellant categorically stated in his evidence that the pre-emptor got his name mutated and in support of such statement he produced and filed the certified copy of the Mutation Khatian, which has been proved and marked as Exhibit-'Kha', without any objection from the pre-emptor, the pre-emptor or anyone now cannot raise any objection as to the admissibility of the same in evidence. The objection as to admissibility of any evidence/document is to be taken at the first instance. No objection having been raised at the time of proving "Exhibit-Kha", none can challenge the same at- later stage. The proceeding of Mutation Khatian and opening of a new/separate khatian pursuant to the said proceeding and the order passed therein is a public document under section 74 of the Evidence Act. Certified copy of such public document can be produced and accepted in the court as a secondary evidence. When the original is a public document under section 74 of the Evidence Act and the original is a document of which a certified copy is permitted by the Act or by any other law in force in Bangladesh to be given in evidence the same may be given/filed in a Court and unless any objection is raised to such document when the same is being filed the same is very much admissible in evidence. This view finds support in the case of Hazi Waziullah alias Waziullah Miah and others Vs. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Noakhali and Assistant Custodian of Vested and Non Resident Property and others, reported in 41 DLR(AD)97.</u>

<u>16. Under such circumstances, when the pre-emptor denied opening of new khatian the burden is upon him to prove that the evidence produced by pre-emptee is not correct. The established principle of law is that the burden of proof lies upon the person who denies the 'public document'. In the present case, the certified copy of the Mutation Khatian is a public document and when the pre-emptor denied the same the burden is upon him to prove that the same is not genuine as provided under section 103 of the Evidence Act. But the pre-emptor did not take any step to do the same nor the trial Court called for the record of the mutation case to justify the claim of the pre-emptor. Rather the trial Court as well as the High Court Division disbelieved the certified copy as well as the Mutation without calling for the original record of the said mutation case. As such the pre-emptee appellant rightly pointed out that for determination as to whether there was separate holding opened vide mutation case the trial Court should have called for the record of the mutation case and in not doing so, we are of the view that the finding of the trial Court as well as those of the High Court Division on this point is not correct.</u>

17. Moreover, when the pre-emptor respondent No.1 has no right to file the pre-emption case over the case land for the reasons as stated above, the judgment of thee trial Court as well as the High Court Division is not proper.

<u>18. On the other hand from the judgment of the lower appellate Court it appears that it held that the preemptor has no right to file the pre-emption case over the case land because of the fact that the pre-emptee appellant, Dr. Forman Ali Miah, when purchased the case land the applicant Nizamuddin was not the co-sharer tenant in the case jote and further held that the pre-emptee has residence contiguous to the case land whereas the applicant Nizamuddin has no such residence contiguous to the case land. The Court of appeal below further held that Kuddus Mollah also transferred some land from the case jote to one Abdul Kader on the same day i.e. on 15.6.1994 but the applicant-Nizamuddin, did not raise any objection to that transfer. Considering all these aspects the Court of appeal rightly allowed the appeal upon setting aside the order of pre-emption which the High Court Division failed to consider in its true perspective.</u>

19. For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove we hold that the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute and thereby allowing the pre-emption case by the impugned judgment and order upon setting aside the judgment of the lower appellate court which is based on proper appreciation of fact and law and as such the impugned judgment is required to be interfered with.

20. Hence, we find merit in the submissions of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

21. Accordingly, this civil appeal is allowed and the judgment and order complained of herein passed by the High court Division is set aside. However, there will be no order as to cost.

End.
